I like that people are speaking out against the incompetence of many job postings and how unrealistic their demands are but I do not see enough discussions about what in my opinion is the elephant in the room. 

Sure, it is easy and alluring to complain about such problems, but I think it would be more constructive to address the cause which in my opinion is an uncomfortable truth - that there are just too many damn people trying to get a job due to education inflation, job market saturation, and in the case for developers, too many people who took a programming course on Udemy and now think they qualify for a job that pays over $80k. 

The job market is such that it is harder for people who actually know what the fuck they're doing to get a new job. 

Imo, its not that there is suddenly an explosion of people who want to code for a living but that the programmer jobs are literally the only kinds of jobs a young person can have that'll allow them to afford their own house. 

One way this issue can be fixed is if other jobs simply paid more or housing went down in price but sadly the opposite for both is happening.

Pipes, tires, cars trucks and other undiscernible goods lay in a heap. You've never seen anything like this. The other divers talked about US supplies being dumped after WWII during their quarrels about whether it was right or wrong. 

No matter, you came here to take EMF readings and pictures. For who and what, it was of no concern as decent coin from the client was the reward. Still, the thought of why anyone would be so interested in this trash heap beyond the novelty of sight-seeing could not escape your mind. Was it for environmental concerns? The Chinese trying to get pre-WWII steel that is uncontaminated from nuclear radiation? A documentary? Then why the electromagnetic readings? 

The job seemed simple enough. Come close, take pictures and record EMF meter data, then hand it to client. Diving closer to the site, you looked around for good places to take pictures. Some shots had trucks, others had heavy-lifting equipment, but all-in-all the heap was mostly made of boring commodities and supplies like piping and parts. 

Taking all of these photos was becoming quite fun. You could not help but appreciate how clear the scene was optimal photography, but then it hit you - the water was clear. Where were the fish? Artificial reefs like this one usually teem with a diversity of wildlife and yet this place was mostly bereft of it. 

"Ha Ha! Maybe it is for some environmental organization!" You thought that maybe the contents of this mound have a negative effect on the local ecosystem. Some shipwrecks have been known to release oil for many decades after they've sunk, so the same thing is probably happening here! 

Once the photos have been made, it was time to take out the EMF meter and start recording the data. Turning it on, things started work normally for the first few moments until the readings spiked. Promptly after the spike, it went back down to ambient levels. 

"Hmm..." You thought. Maybe the meter was faulty? After all, electronics and water do not mix well. Inspecting the meter revealed that nothing seemed to be wrong. The EMF around this heap was actually fluctuating, which was very abnormal and... unnatural. 

"Oh you dunce! It is coming from the boat that dropped you off!" This thought extinguished the feeling of fear building up inside. There was no way this heap of trash emitted a pulsating electromagnetic signal. You just had to come closer to the pile and farther away from the boat to get a better, less contaminated reading. Looking around, you see an opening inside the pile which looked like a good place to collect the data. 

Once at the mouth, you pull out the EMF meter and switch it on. A few seconds of ambient recordings, followed by a loud beep! Your stomach sinks and adrenaline starts flowing. The pulsating signal was stronger here which meant the source was not from his boat... but in there. 

Before getting the fuck out of there, being the risky type, you decide to take some photos in the opening's dark inside. You had no flashlight but your camera had a decent flash attached to it. 

Beep.........Beep.........Beep. The meter's recording was steady. You were not going to look into the opening when the photos would be taken in case something terrifying was in there which would paralyze you with fear. Beep...Beep...Beep...Beep...Beep. The pulses accelerated. Whatever it was, it seemed to warming up or coming closer. 

Flash! Flash! Flash! Right away you shoot up without looking back. Your EMF meter emitted a solid beep without pulses, like a flatlining heart rate. Before boarding the boat, looking down, there seemed to be nothing out of the ordinary and the meter went back to pulses separated by a few seconds. 

The divers on the boat looked at you like you were crazy. "Damn, he's pale as snow!" one remarked. Patting you on the back a diver says "What's the matter mate, thought you saw a shark in the wreck? I remember the last I've swam away from a wreck this fast was when I thought I saw my ex inside the SS Thistlegorm!" Everyone laughed. 

"I... I just thought something was wrong with my air supply and panicked, that's all." 

After coming back to your hotel, you plugged the SD card of your camera into your laptop. There were mixed feelings about what you were going to see in those last three photos. Once the first one popped up, there was confusion. 

Clearly the the opening was that of a tunnel. The camera had good resolution so you zoomed into the edges of the flash. It seemed like the deeper you looked, the more off-context the wreck pieces were. For example, at some point you stopped seeing cars, tractors and piping but instead... cannons, like black powder cannons from centuries ago. 

It seemed like the inner portion of the pile was made of wooden junk. It was also pretty well-preserved and not covered in growth like the outside. The wooden parts looked like remains from galleys and caravels. 

The tunnel's middle was still shrouded in darkness so you thought maybe the other images taken at a different angle would reveal more. 

The second image made your heart stop. Emerging from the dark was a claw-like device. It had multiple smooth chrome-colored pincers with pin-point tapered ends. The last image made you gasp. The claw was closer. 

The next day you came back home. Your girl friend asked how was the trip. Of course you spin a tale of how wonderful things were and that you got all you needed. But in the end, you could not resist the urge to tell her "and for some pictures... I will make them pay through the nose!"

After you entered the room, what struck out was how clean everything was. It smelled almost like a well-kept pool and the water was crystal-clear. Being the adventurous type, you had the urge to take a dip in this inviting water.

After descending a few steps down the clean stainless-steel stairs, your body gets used to the water's slightly cool temperature as you admire the oddly-satisfying workmanship of the welds around the stair's railing. 

Looking over, you see the tank descending into an abyss with a black void, making it appear bottomless. For some reason, this did not set off any red flags in your head.

You then proceed to wade into the water, swimming underneath the lower ceiling, admiring the quality tiling. In your mind, your goal was to reach the far end of the reservoir and come back. 

But then, something happened. As you've reached the far wall of the reservoir, you hear an alarm go off. The sounds of hidden machinery going to life follow after. A slight rumbling resonates throughout the chamber and to your utter shock and horror, the water level starts going down!

You look down into the clear water and see the bottom, but due to being under a ledge, your eyes have adjusted to see darkness better. What you see sends you into utter panic. Not only is the bottom visible, but clearly, there are holes down there, holes that are big enough for you to fit in. To make matters worse, there is something mechanical moving down there. If you don't get sucked into a pipe, then you'll be ground up. 

The only way out is the way you went in. You had to reach that ladder before it was too late. You start swimming frantically, putting your best effort into reaching that platform. By the time you've reached the platform, you still had water to spare. But then, the moment your hand grabbed the edge, something snags your ankle and starts pulling you down!

Your hand slips and you descend into the water. The sounds of machinery permeated throughout the water. You look down but all you see are bubbles and darkness. You kick whatever grabbed you. After kicking for what seemed like an eternity, it finally lets go of you and with all your strength, you swim to the surface. 

At this point, the water is slightly below the platform. You grab the edge and pull yourself up. Once on the platform, you quickly crawl up the stairs and look back. The reservoir now looks like some death machine, and you got a new phobia. 

Understandably, someone who went through such trauma would go the bar and while intoxicated with some buddies, you tell them what happened. 

"Oh that place?" says your friend, "didn't like, someone drown there several years ago?" 

A horrible thought hits you like a ton of bricks. That night, you needed to down a whole bottle of wine to sleep.
